In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there are many reasons for delaying the introduction of characters.
the majority of teachers and students in the study supported immediate character introduction (I.C.I.).
the majority of teachers and students in the U.S., in both DCI and ICI programs, did not favor delayed introduction of Chinese characters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the majority of the CFL programs in our study did not delay the introduction of Chinese characters; that the majority of teachers and students in our study believed that speaking and understanding were the most important and the most difficult skills, respectively; and that most CFL teachers and students in the study did not favor alternative ways to replace the handwriting component of character writing even though they considered character handwriting as the most difficult skill to learn.
the results of the study indicate that the majority (about 80%) of CFL programs in the United States do not delay the introduction of Chinese characters in the first year of CFL courses.

we found that the majority of programs do not delay teaching characters, that most teachers and students believed speaking and listening were more important than reading and writing, and that most teachers and most students did not favor alternatives to the handwriting of Chinese characters, even though handwriting is considered the most difficult skill.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of teachers and students do not support delayed character introduction in CFL programs in the United States.
the timing structure of Chinese character teaching should be decided by the teachers and students in the classroom based on a variety of factors.
the teaching of Chinese characters in U.S. post-secondary institutions has not yet reached a point of maturity where a consensus on the timing of introducing Chinese characters can be reached.
